script:
Your Daily AI Press Review — June 03, 2026: Capital War.

Alphabet is raising $80 billion in equity — the largest single fundraising in market history — including a $10 billion direct stake sold to Berkshire Hathaway, as its 2026 capital spending heads toward $190 billion. On the same day, Anthropic filed confidentially for its IPO at a $965 billion post-money valuation, even as a Bain survey of nearly 1,000 companies shows 40 percent of AI adopters are seeing cost savings below 10 percent. Off the radar, ByteDance's Volcano Engine just revised its MaaS revenue target to 150 billion yuan for 2026 — ten times its actual 2025 revenue — driven almost entirely by a single video model.

Alphabet is raising $80 billion in equity to fund AI infrastructure, in what analysts are calling the largest equity fundraising ever executed. The structure includes $30 billion in underwritten public offerings, a $40 billion at-the-market program, and a $10 billion direct share sale to Berkshire Hathaway. Alphabet's 2026 capital expenditure is projected at $190 billion. The fundraising comes as the company faces unprecedented customer demand for compute, and it signals that the infrastructure arms race has moved decisively into equity markets rather than debt.

Anthropic filed confidentially for a US IPO just days after closing a Series H that valued the company at $965 billion post-money — up from $380 billion in February, a near-tripling in under four months. The company did not disclose a target IPO valuation. The filing lands as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman publicly called corporate concern over AI costs 'the most fair criticism of AI so far,' and as a Bain survey of nearly 1,000 companies found that 40 percent report AI cost savings below 10 percent — a direct headwind for Anthropic's enterprise revenue story ahead of its public debut.

Microsoft launched seven new in-house AI models at Build 2026, headlined by MAI-Thinking-1, a one-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts reasoning model with 35 billion active parameters, available initially to select enterprise partners. A second model, MAI-Code-1-Flash, carries 137 billion parameters with 5 billion active and is rolling out now to GitHub Copilot users in Visual Studio Code. Both models were trained end-to-end by Microsoft on commercially licensed data, without distillation from third-party models — a deliberate positioning move as licensing disputes intensify across the industry.

Microsoft also announced Project Solara at Build 2026, a new operating system purpose-built for AI agent hardware. It's built on Android, not Windows, and Microsoft demonstrated two concept devices — a desk unit and a badge form factor. Separately, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced a unified technology stack for deploying agentic AI across Windows devices, cloud, and on-premise environments, deepening a hardware-software integration that positions both companies at the center of enterprise agent infrastructure.

OpenAI's Codex now has more than 4 million weekly active users, up more than five times since the desktop app launched in February. Knowledge workers — non-developers using Codex for documents, dashboards, and data analysis — now represent roughly one-fifth of the user base and are growing more than three times faster than developers. OpenAI shared the figures exclusively with Axios ahead of a broader report, framing Codex as a tool for making sense of the accumulated 'workplace artifacts' siloed across enterprise software stacks.

OpenAI's latest frontier models, including its newest GPT and Codex coding agent, are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock with pay-per-token pricing, built-in security controls, and governance tooling. The listing on Bedrock gives AWS enterprise customers direct access to OpenAI's most capable models without leaving the AWS security perimeter — a significant distribution move that puts OpenAI's models alongside Anthropic's Claude and other providers on the same managed inference platform.

Chinese AI company MiniMax released its M3 model, billed as the first open-weight model combining top-tier coding performance, a one-million-token context window, and native multimodality in a single architecture. The release comes as MiniMax and peer company Zhipu — also known as Knowledge Atlas Technology — both filed for Hong Kong IPOs before pursuing mainland China listings, reversing the traditional dual-listing sequence to anchor valuations with global investors first.

Tencent shares surged more than 10 percent on June 2, the largest single-day gain since January 2021, pushing its market capitalization to about 4.4 trillion Hong Kong dollars. The catalyst was a Financial Times report that Tencent is testing an AI agent prototype for WeChat, which has 1.4 billion active users, with a compliance filing for public launch expected as soon as this month. The same day, Meituan's CEO confirmed that its AI assistant 'Xiaomei' will integrate with Tencent's Yuanbao app to enable one-stop food delivery transactions.

Anthropic expanded its cybersecurity program Project Glasswing, tripling access to its Mythos model from 50 organizations to 150. Mythos is Anthropic's specialized cybersecurity model, and the expansion comes directly after the White House signed a narrowed executive order on AI and cybersecurity — one that stops short of compelling AI companies to share model information but acknowledges that models like Mythos have revealed 'shocking' vulnerabilities. Microsoft's MDASH security platform also exited preview at Build 2026 with more than 100 specialized threat-hunting AI agents.

On deployments. Travelers Insurance deployed an AI-powered Claim Assistant built with OpenAI countrywide, providing 24/7 claims guidance and scaling support capacity during peak demand periods without disclosed headcount additions. The deployment covers the full claims filing workflow — intake, status updates, and customer communication — and represents one of the largest announced insurance AI rollouts in the US market, with Travelers serving tens of millions of policyholders across personal and commercial lines.

Macy's launched Ask Macy's, a conversational shopping assistant built on Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer platform, targeting the roughly 70 percent of online shopping carts that are abandoned before purchase. The assistant lets shoppers describe what they want in natural language and returns personalized product recommendations in real time. Macy's is betting that conversational AI can move the cart abandonment rate — a figure that has resisted improvement from discount pop-ups, email reminders, and loyalty programs for more than a decade.

Robinhood launched an agentic AI system for stock trading, allowing users to instruct the platform in natural language to execute trades, set conditions, and manage positions. The deployment makes Robinhood one of the first retail brokerages to offer fully agentic execution — not just research or recommendations — to its user base of tens of millions of accounts. Interactive Brokers separately announced agentic trading through a direct integration with Anthropic's Claude, giving institutional and active retail clients a second major platform for AI-driven order execution.

Realtor.com launched RealAssist AI, a conversational property search tool built on Google's Gemini, that lets buyers describe requirements in plain language and receive listings with integrated MLS data, affordability calculations, and agent connections — replacing the traditional filter interface entirely. The tool is currently in beta ahead of a broader rollout. The launch targets a 2026 US housing market where transaction volumes remain constrained, making search-to-conversion efficiency a direct revenue lever for the platform.

Indian IT services firms TCS, Infosys, and Wipro collectively crossed 300,000 Microsoft Copilot users, according to reporting from DT Next, marking a significant enterprise adoption milestone for the three companies that together employ roughly 1.4 million people. The figure represents a small fraction of total headcount but signals that large-scale Copilot licensing deals are now live and measurable across India's biggest outsourcing players — companies whose productivity economics are directly tied to AI-assisted software delivery.

Jubilant FoodWorks, the operator of Domino's in India, launched a generative AI chatbot for customer ordering during its Q4 FY26 earnings period, as the company reported slowing delivery growth against food aggregator competition. The chatbot is designed to handle order intake and upselling at scale. Jubilant's deployment is notable because it comes under direct competitive pressure — aggregators are outpacing Domino's own delivery channel growth — making AI-driven conversion a defensive as well as offensive tool.

WeRide and Uber jointly announced plans to launch Spain's first commercial robotaxi pilot in Madrid, making it the 12th city in WeRide's global robotaxi network. The service has support from the regional government of Madrid and is scheduled to launch before the end of 2026. The partnership marks WeRide's first European collaboration with Uber and extends a model the two companies have already deployed across multiple Asian and Middle Eastern cities.

On tools. Uber capped employee spending on agentic AI coding tools at $1,500 per tool per month after exhausting its annual AI software budget ahead of schedule. The cap applies per tool, meaning an employee using multiple agentic coding platforms can spend $1,500 on each. This is the first publicly disclosed hard spending ceiling from a major technology company on agentic coding software — giving CFOs and procurement teams a concrete benchmark for what uncapped AI coding access costs at enterprise scale.

Amazon Web Services published a technical guide for accelerating LLM model loading using GPUDirect on FSx for Lustre combined with TurboQuant quantization, targeting the latency bottleneck that occurs when loading large models into GPU high-bandwidth memory. The combination allows practitioners to reduce model load times and expand effective context windows on existing GPU infrastructure without hardware upgrades. AWS framed the technique as directly applicable to teams iterating on inference deployments where startup latency is a production constraint.

Amazon Bedrock's AgentCore Gateway now supports OAuth code flow as an inbound authorization mechanism for MCP servers, enabling each AI agent request to be authenticated against an organization's existing identity provider. The capability means enterprise teams can deploy MCP-based agents with the same identity and access management controls they apply to human users — closing a significant security gap that had made agentic deployments difficult to approve in regulated environments like banking and healthcare.

Snowflake introduced Horizon Context at its developer conference, a feature designed to give AI agents a shared semantic understanding of a company's data — including table definitions, business metrics, and data lineage — so that multiple agents operating across the same Snowflake environment produce consistent answers. The update addresses a core enterprise complaint: that different AI agents querying the same data warehouse return contradictory results because they lack a common business context layer.

MIT researchers released ChartNet, a new training dataset designed to improve the ability of vision-language models to interpret charts and data visualizations accurately. Models trained on ChartNet show measurably better performance on business chart comprehension tasks — reading trend lines, comparing series, and extracting specific values — compared to models trained on general image-text data. The dataset is being released publicly, making it immediately usable for teams fine-tuning models for financial analysis, reporting, or scientific figure interpretation.

One signal to watch. Enterprise AI cost control is hardening from a CFO concern into a structural constraint. Uber capped agentic coding spend at $1,500 per tool per month after burning through its annual budget. A Bain survey of nearly 1,000 companies found 40 percent reporting AI cost savings below 10 percent. Anthropic's own early investor flagged to Axios that enterprise clients are waking up to how much they're spending on Claude. These three data points — from a tech operator, a consulting survey, and an insider — converge on the same dynamic: AI spend is now large enough to trigger formal governance.

The open-weight model gap between China and the US is narrowing on context length but persisting on benchmark leadership. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra is now ranked the most capable open US model by Artificial Analysis, yet Chinese models still lead the overall open-weight rankings. MiniMax M3 launched with a one-million-token context window — a capability no US open-weight model currently matches. Two Chinese AI companies, MiniMax and Zhipu, are simultaneously pursuing Hong Kong IPOs before mainland listings, using global capital markets to set valuations that domestic exchanges would price lower. The capital and capability race is running in parallel.

AI hardware memory constraints are attracting serious capital and architectural innovation simultaneously. Startup Majestic Labs is developing the Prometheus server with up to 128 terabytes of LPDDR6 memory — more than 60 times the memory in NVIDIA's current flagship DGX B300 rack — using a proprietary copper cable interface effective up to one meter. Separately, SK Hynix crossed a one-trillion-dollar market capitalization on the back of high-bandwidth memory demand, joining Samsung and TSMC in Asia's trillion-dollar chip club. The memory wall is now a recognized bottleneck with both startup and incumbent capital flowing toward it.

Off the radar. ByteDance's Volcano Engine — the cloud and AI services arm of TikTok's parent — quietly revised its MaaS revenue target for 2026 to 150 billion yuan, up from 100 billion yuan set just six months ago, and ten times the 15 billion yuan it actually earned in 2025. The revision is driven almost entirely by Seedance 2.0, a video generation model that is now producing more than 10 billion yuan in monthly revenue on its own. Token consumption on Volcano Engine is still growing at nearly 40 percent month-over-month. The Seedance 2.0 API is not yet fully available outside China — meaning these numbers were achieved in a constrained market.

India's Sarvam AI is preparing a major commercial push into voice agents for public deployment, according to Inc42. Sarvam is a homegrown Indian AI company focused on Indic languages, and its voice stack is designed to handle regional dialects at scale — a capability gap that global models including OpenAI and Google have not closed for most of India's 22 scheduled languages. xAI is separately recruiting Chinese-language AI tutors globally to improve Grok's Mandarin and dialect capabilities, signaling that non-English language quality is now a competitive frontier that major labs are actively staffing.

A French regional government — the Indre-et-Loire department, with its council voting in Tours on May 29 — banned ChatGPT and Google Gemini for staff use while explicitly authorizing Microsoft Copilot Chat, which is natively integrated into the Microsoft 365 suite the department already uses. The charter also prohibits entering sensitive or confidential data into any AI tool, including Copilot. This is one of the first documented cases of a European public institution making a formal, named vendor selection between competing AI assistants — a governance model that other regional governments are likely to replicate.

Tokyo-based healthtech startup I.W.G raised $1.8 million in a pre-Series A round led by Golden Gate Ventures, with Antler participating, to build an AI-driven interoperability platform that maps and routes clinical data across incompatible hospital systems and languages across Asia. The funding is small but the problem is large: Asia's healthcare data infrastructure is fragmented across dozens of incompatible national systems, and no major US or European health AI company has built a cross-border clinical data routing layer for the region. I.W.G is positioning as the connective tissue before larger players arrive.

On the research front. NVIDIA released Cosmos 3, a family of omnimodal world models that jointly process and generate language, images, video, audio, and action sequences within a single mixture-of-transformers architecture. At release, Cosmos 3's post-trained models ranked as the best open-source text-to-image and image-to-video models on Artificial Analysis, and the best policy model on RoboArena. NVIDIA is releasing code, model checkpoints, synthetic datasets, and evaluation benchmarks under the Linux Foundation's OpenMDW license — making Cosmos 3 the most capable open physical AI foundation released to date.

Turing Award winner Richard Sutton published a pointed argument that pure generative AI cannot do real science because it lacks the ability to evaluate its own outputs. Without a built-in evaluation loop, Sutton argues, any novel result a generative model produces is immediately lost — it cannot be recognized as novel, tested, or built upon. He cites AlphaGo and AlphaProof as examples of systems that do have evaluation loops and therefore can be genuinely creative. The argument has direct implications for AI research automation: systems that generate hypotheses without verification mechanisms cannot replace the scientific method.

Researchers published MT-OSC, a framework that reduces token counts in multi-turn LLM conversations by up to 72 percent in ten-turn dialogues, by condensing chat history in the background without disrupting the user experience. The system uses a Condenser Agent with a lightweight Decider module to selectively retain essential context. Evaluated across 13 state-of-the-art LLMs and multiple multi-turn benchmarks, MT-OSC consistently narrows the performance gap between single-turn and multi-turn interactions — a result that matters directly for enterprise chatbot deployments where long conversation threads degrade both accuracy and cost efficiency.

The PromptSE AI system, reported by News-Medical, predicts drug side effects by reasoning through biological clues rather than pattern-matching on known adverse event databases. The approach allows the model to surface plausible side effects for novel drug candidates where historical data is sparse or absent. For pharmaceutical companies and clinical AI vendors, the capability addresses one of the most expensive failure modes in drug development: late-stage safety surprises that could have been flagged earlier with better biological reasoning tools.
